new_statements.rule_in_words: The only evidence is the acute accents Raffles (1817) printed on his ~48-word Tembora list, which Raffles never explains; Donohue reads them as (erratic) stress marks and observes that, if so, stress falls predominantly on the penultimate syllable (e.g. kutélin, koného, saróne, homóri, kokóre, simári, karáyi, moríhoh). He explicitly says suprasegmentals cannot be securely inferred from the corpus.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (corpus is isolated words only).
new_statements.exceptions: None discussed by Donohue; the accent marking is called 'erratic' (some polysyllables unaccented, e.g. seena, yelai, maimpo, naido). A few accented forms in Raffles' list are not obviously penultimate depending on syllabification of vowel sequences/hyphens (kálae, báta-in, óna-yit, gónong vs gonóre), which Donohue does not comment on.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms only: single words elicited in 1810s and printed in a comparative vocabulary; no phrases or clauses exist for the language. Statement is an inference from a philological source, hedged as conditional.
new_statements.identity_note: Single variety; Raffles spells it 'Tembóra', Zollinger 'Tambora/Tembora'. Language extinct since the 1815 eruption; entire corpus is Raffles' 1817 ~48-word list (Appendix F, vol. II), so Donohue 2007 is and will remain the only linguistic analysis. Glottocode tamb1257, ISO xxt.
